summary: Proposes several elliptic curve domain parameters over prime fields for cryptographic use, consistent with international standards and usable in X.509 certificates, CRLs and key exchange. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some secret codes use special curved shapes. This hands out a set of agreed shapes anyone can use.

subtitle: Seven sets of elliptic curve parameters for use in cryptography, generated to be immune to known attacks.

tldr.problem: Existing elliptic curve standards have limitations: curve parameters were generated ad-hoc, not verifiably pseudo-randomly; they do not cover all commonly needed key lengths; and proofs that they resist known attacks are missing.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes seven new elliptic curves over prime fields, with bit lengths of 160, 192, 224, 256, 320, 384, and 512 bits. The curves are generated in a verifiably pseudo-random, systematic way and selected to meet strict security requirements, including immunity to pairing attacks and trace-one attacks, and prime group order.
tldr.outcome: The Brainpool curves became widely used alternatives to older standards, particularly for applications requiring high assurance. They are compliant with international standards and suitable for X.509 certificates, TLS, IKE, XML signatures, and other cryptographic protocols.

today: RFC 5639 is an Informational standards document. The Brainpool curves are specified in international standards (ISO/IEC, ETSI, German standards), widely implemented, and used in TLS, IKE, X.509 certificates, and other protocols, particularly in Europe and for high-assurance applications.

sections.title: Why New Elliptic Curves
sections.content:
Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) uses points on a mathematical curve to create cryptographic keys and signatures. Several standards already define elliptic curve parameters (ANSI, FIPS, SECG). However, the RFC identifies several problems with those standards:

Most existing curve parameters were chosen ad-hoc rather than using a verifiable process. Their base field primes have special forms designed for fast arithmetic, but this introduces patent risks and reduces confidence in security. No rigorous proofs are given that the curves resist known cryptanalytic attacks. Parameters do not cover all bit lengths that match symmetric key sizes (for example, there is a 521-bit curve but no 512-bit one). Some curves have non-trivial cofactors, requiring additional security checks in applications.

The RFC responds by specifying new elliptic curve domain parameters covering the gap in bit lengths, generated in a systematic and reproducible pseudo-random way, with rigorous security proofs, and selected to meet strict requirements.
sections.eli5: Old curve formulas were chosen somewhat randomly and no one proved they were safe enough. These new curves are chosen carefully with proofs that they work.

sections.title: Security and Technical Requirements
sections.content:
The Brainpool curves meet strict security requirements:

Immunity to pairing attacks: Certain elliptic curves allow an attacker to embed the curve's subgroup into a larger field where discrete logarithm attacks are faster. The Brainpool curves require that this embedding degree l satisfy (q-1)/l < 100, making such attacks infeasible.

No trace-one curves: Anomalous curves (trace one) are susceptible to efficient discrete logarithm attacks. The Brainpool curves exclude them.

Large class number: The endomorphism ring's class number must exceed 10^7, providing additional defense against potential lifting attacks.

Prime group order: The group of points has prime order (cofactor 1) to prevent small-subgroup attacks.

Pseudo-random generation: Curve parameters are derived systematically from seeds, using a method described in the RFC's appendix. This allows anyone to verify the generation process and rules out ad-hoc choices.

Technical requirements include: a prime field modulus p ≡ 3 mod 4 for efficient point compression, curves isomorphic to a form with coefficient A = -3 for fast arithmetic, a non-special prime (avoiding special forms), and the group size less than the field size.
sections.eli5: The curves pass multiple checks: they are hard to attack, they are generated systematically so no one cheated, and they are efficient to compute.

sections.title: The Seven Brainpool Curves
sections.content:
The RFC specifies seven elliptic curves over prime fields, one for each of seven bit lengths: 160, 192, 224, 256, 320, 384, and 512 bits. Each bit length corresponds to a different security level appropriate for different symmetric key sizes.

For each primary curve (identified as, for example, brainpoolP256r1 for the 256-bit curve), the RFC also specifies a twisted curve (for example, brainpoolP256t1). A twisted curve is an isomorphic variant computed via a mathematical transformation; it offers the same security as the primary curve but allows implementations to use different arithmetic.

For each curve, the RFC provides:

  • p: the prime that defines the base field.
  • A and B: the coefficients of the elliptic curve equation y^2 = x^3 + A*x + B mod p.
  • G: the base point (generator) on the curve, given as (x, y) coordinates.
  • q: the prime order of the group generated by G.
  • h: the cofactor, always 1 for Brainpool curves.
  • For twisted curves, Z: the isomorphism coefficient.

All parameters are given as hexadecimal numbers to ensure exact precision across implementations.
sections.eli5: There are seven different curve recipes, ranging from 160 bits (small) to 512 bits (large), each with the ingredients (p, A, B, G, q) needed to set up the math.

sections.title: Using Brainpool Curves in Practice
sections.content:
The Brainpool curves are designed to be used in existing cryptographic protocols: TLS for secure web connections, IKE for virtual private networks, X.509 certificates for digital identity, XML signatures for document authentication, and the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) for encrypted email and data.

Each Brainpool curve is assigned an Object Identifier (OID), a unique numeric label used in certificates and protocol messages to identify which curve is in use. For example, the 256-bit primary curve brainpoolP256r1 is identified by the OID 1.3.36.3.3.2.8.1.1.1.

When a cryptographic application creates a key pair using a Brainpool curve, it uses the curve's base point G and a random private key d to compute a public key. Signatures and key agreements follow standard ECC algorithms; the Brainpool curves themselves are purely parameter sets, not new algorithms.

An application can choose which Brainpool curve to use based on the desired security level: 160-bit curves provide security equivalent to 80-bit symmetric encryption, 256-bit curves equivalent to 128-bit symmetric encryption, and 512-bit curves equivalent to 256-bit symmetric encryption.
sections.eli5: Pick one of the seven curves depending on how secure you need to be, and use it in your certificate, encrypted message, or login system.
